clinicalPearls: Knock knees are a normal stage of lower-limb development, typically most pronounced around three to four years of age as part of the physiological swing from infantile varus toward adult alignment
Physiological genu valgum is symmetrical and painless, occurs in a child of normal stature, and improves spontaneously toward the mild adult valgus by about seven years
The intermalleolar distance measured with the knees together is used to quantify and follow the deformity over time
Persistence beyond seven to eight years, worsening, marked severity, or asymmetry suggests a pathological rather than physiological cause
Rickets, renal osteodystrophy, skeletal dysplasia, and post-traumatic physeal injury are important pathological causes and are often accompanied by short stature or other features
Excessive valgus can contribute to patellofemoral maltracking, an awkward gait, and anterior knee pain in older children

Physiological valgus needs only reassurance and observation, while significant pathological deformity in a growing child may be corrected by guided growth (hemiepiphysiodesis) or, at maturity, osteotomy
reference.pathophysiology: Genu valgum is an inward (valgus) angulation at the knee so that the knees approximate while the ankles separate. It is a normal phase of skeletal maturation, following the earlier varus of infancy, and remodels predictably toward the modest physiological valgus of adulthood. Pathological valgum develops when growth is disturbed: metabolic bone disease such as rickets or renal osteodystrophy softens and deforms the growing bone; skeletal dysplasias alter physeal development; and asymmetric growth after trauma, infection, or a proximal tibial fracture (as in the classic post-fracture valgus) produces localised deformity. Persistent severe valgus laterally displaces the extensor mechanism and predisposes to patellofemoral problems and, in the long term, medial compartment overload.
additionalDifferentials: Physiological genu valgum of early childhood
Skeletal dysplasia such as spondyloepiphyseal or multiple epiphyseal dysplasia
Post-traumatic valgus following a proximal tibial metaphyseal fracture
Post-infective or post-injury physeal growth disturbance
Syndromic causes such as Ellis-van Creveld or Morquio syndrome
additionalInvestigations: Serial measurement of the intermalleolar distance and clinical alignment
Standing full-length lower-limb radiographs with assessment of the mechanical axis
Assessment of stature and proportion against growth charts
Biochemical screen for rickets and renal function where a metabolic cause is suspected
Skeletal survey or genetic evaluation if a dysplasia is considered
Review of any history of trauma, infection, or previous fracture near the knee
redFlags: Deformity persisting or worsening beyond about seven to eight years of age
Short stature or disproportion suggesting a dysplasia or metabolic disease
Knee pain, patellar instability, or gait disturbance
History of trauma, infection, or metabolic disorder affecting the growing bone
reference.prognosis: Physiological knock knees resolve spontaneously and carry an excellent prognosis, whereas untreated pathological valgus can progress to fixed deformity, patellofemoral instability, and later degenerative change, though guided growth in the skeletally immature child gives good correction.
pitfalls: Over-investigating a normal child during the physiological valgus phase
Failing to recognise pathological valgus persisting beyond the expected age
Missing rickets, renal disease, or a dysplasia signalled by short stature
Overlooking post-traumatic valgus after an apparently minor proximal tibial fracture
Deferring guided growth until skeletal maturity, when the opportunity for gentle correction is lost
